value: red clover emitted about three-fold more total volatiles after caterpillar feeding than undamaged plants; five compounds rose (1-octen-3-ol, (E)- and (Z)-beta-ocimene, (E)-beta-caryophyllene, DMNT) and methyl salicylate was not detected; monoterpenes went from about 3% of the blend in controls to about 48% under herbivory; neighbour composition significantly changed total emission (Dactylis glomerata raised it) and red clover growing with Geranium pratense emitted significantly less DMNT, with a significant herbivory x G. pratense interaction for DMNT; plant species richness did not affect emission of the red clover focal plant (null), although whole-community emission rose with richness
method: push-pull headspace collection, 1 h between 1000 and 1300 h, from the focal red clover plant and from whole pots
conditions: Every pot held six plants: the monoculture was six T. pratense, mixtures added Geranium pratense and/or Dactylis glomerata, so the focal plant always had neighbours; 48 pots in six blocks (four compositions x herbivory or control, eight pots a block); focal plant an outer plant; herbivory was three 3rd-instar Spodoptera littoralis (starved 8 h) feeding 24 h on the focal plant in a bag; seedlings raised about 7 weeks; climate chamber; seed from Rieger Hofmann, no cultivar named

source.authors: Rose N. Kigathi, Wolfgang W. Weisser, Michael Reichelt, Jonathan Gershenzon, Sybille B. Unsicker

quote: As numerous other studies before, we found a strong effect of insect herbivory of the VOC emission of the plant attacked.
note: Full text read through WebFetch summaries; the quote is a Discussion sentence confirmed verbatim on two fetches, chosen because no Results or Abstract sentence of 125 characters or fewer states the herbivore effect (the Results sentence with the three-fold rise is about 230 characters and starts 'Upon caterpillar damage, total VOC emission from T. pratense was found to be three-fold higher than the emission of control'). No issue number is printed on the pages read; Crossref lists issue 1 (verified on Crossref). Accepted name: POWO urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:523575-1 (accepted), WFO wfo-0000213053 (accepted, June 2025). Herbivore-induced response of a living plant (owner reading of sense_chemical). Audit 196 refile: corrects 'grown alone', carries G. pratense DMNT decrease and richness null.

value: black poplar emitted herbivore-induced volatiles after gypsy moth feeding: cyclic monoterpenes rose only about two-fold, whereas (E)-beta-ocimene rose about 7000-fold, DMNT about 4000-fold and (E)-beta-caryophyllene about 250-fold; four compounds ((E)-beta-caryophyllene, 3-methylbutyraldoxime, myrcene, nerolidol) differed between 5th-instar L. dispar and L. populi damage and were all higher after L. dispar; four compounds ((E)-beta-caryophyllene, 3-methylbutyraldoxime, (Z)-3-hexenol, nerolidol) were higher after L. dispar alone than after the mixed-species treatment, and the mixed treatment did not differ significantly from L. populi alone (null); feeding intensity significantly affected most monoterpenes, nerolidol, (E)-beta-caryophyllene, most nitrogen-containing compounds and (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate, while DMNT, benzyl alcohol and benzene ethanol were not affected by feeding intensity or by herbivore identity and stage
method: dynamic headspace volatile collection from young trees: a 96 h time course in 6 h intervals, and a species and stage experiment collected for 4 h at 48 to 52 h with caterpillars still feeding
conditions: Time course: 15 4th-instar Lymantria dispar per tree, removed after 48 h, 10 trees per treatment (herbivory or control), trees about 2 months and 40 cm; species and stage experiment: 5 trees per treatment (control, L. dispar 2nd instar about 60 caterpillars, L. dispar 5th instar and Laothoe populi 5th instar 3 to 4 caterpillars each, mixed 2 of each), 3000 mg larval weight a tree, tree age given only as young; trees grown from stem cuttings of old-growth trees, no clone named; climate chamber

value: seeds of the pioneer tree (printed Trema tomentosa) did not germinate in darkness and germinated under both simulated forest-gap light (125 umol m-2 s-1) and simulated understory light (6 umol m-2 s-1); under understory light germination started later (germination start 25 d against 15 d in gap light; mean germination time 29 d against 21.8 d), and final germination, mean time and start differed significantly among the three light conditions; only the temperature requirement was gap-only, since germination in the temperature test occurred only under the 20-30 C gap cycle (93%) and none was reported at constant 30 C or 20/25 C
method: indoor seed germination under simulated gap light, understory light and darkness (14 h light, 10 h dark), plus a separate temperature test
conditions: soil seed bank species of a Hainan Island tropical rain forest; light test 3 replicates of 10 seeds per treatment for Trema; dark below 0.13 umol m-2 s-1; R:FR not measured; the chamber temperature of the light test was not settled by the text read (the summaries differed)

value: leaf GA3 content, measured by HPLC, rose under blue and far-red light and fell under red light (highest under far-red and blue, lowest under red and the 1:1 red:far-red mix), with ABA showing the opposite trend and peaking under red; height rose significantly under blue and 1:2 red:far-red only (p < 0.05), while red, far-red and 1:1 gave no significant height change; the abstract says red light and the 1:1 mix increased root collar diameter, and Results 3.1 reports the greatest root collar diameter under red and the smallest under blue
method: three months of LED light-quality treatments (white, blue, red, far-red, red:far-red 1:1 and 1:2) at equal photon flux; endogenous leaf GA3 and ABA by HPLC
conditions: one-year-old clonal seedlings, 12 h photoperiod, photon flux density printed as 400 'mmol' m-2 s-1 (presumably umol), six seedlings per chamber (n = 6 for growth), hormones on three seedlings per treatment; R:FR values of the mixes not measured

value: seed germination did not differ among white light, red light and darkness (null): the light regimes did not change germination percentage, germination speed index or mean germination time (Tukey, 5%); in the other tests germination percentage also did not differ among substrates or among 20, 25, 30 and 20-30 C, and only germination speed index and mean germination time differed (lowest at 20 C and on germitest paper)
method: germination under white light (transparent box), red light (red cellophane) and darkness (opaque box)
conditions: sand substrate, 25 C in a BOD germinator, four replicates of 25 seeds, completely randomised, dark and red treatments counted under a green safe light, radicle over 2 mm as germinated; seeds from campus trees collected in 2006, wings removed, soaked 12 h

value: seedlings responded to both light level (photon flux density, PFD) and red:far-red ratio (R:FR): internode length rose with greater PFD and with reduced R:FR, though the effects were not large; stem mass per length rose with PFD and fell slightly at low R:FR; leaf allocation fell with rising PFD and also at low R:FR; mean leaf area was reduced by low R:FR and full sunlight; Table 6 marks R:FR significant for stomatal conductance (PFD not significant), palisade cell length (PFD also significant), stomatal density (PFD also significant) and internode length (PFD also significant); growth was highest at 40% sunlight and fell significantly in full sun; the abstract nevertheless says leaf anatomy and physiology were influenced exclusively by PFD, which Table 6 contradicts
method: shadehouse light treatments crossing PFD and R:FR (six treatments including full sun), harvested after 429 to 441 days
conditions: treatments in 12 enclosures in two buildings, 10 seedlings an enclosure; abstract and Table 1 give R:FR 1.25 (high) and 0.25 (low) and PFD 40, 13, 10 and 3% of sun, whereas the Methods text gives 14% PFD at R:FR 1.30, 3% at 1.31 and 10% and 3% at 0.24 and 0.23, so the treatment values differ between abstract, Table 1 and Methods
